1
INTRODUCTION
Congress has not authorized the federal government to create a master 
database of U.S. citizens. Nor does the government possess any dataset capable of 
providing accurate, real-time verification of individuals’ U.S. citizenship status. And 
multiple statutes restrict federal agencies’ ability to use, repurpose, and disclose 
Americans’ sensitive personal information—either within the federal government or 
outside of it. These laws protect Americans from government overreach into their 
private lives and the careless use of their sensitive information held in trust by the 
federal government.
Disregarding these laws, the government has recklessly created an error-laden 
master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans’ privacy and voting 
rights. In 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) and Social Security 
Administration (“SSA”) rapidly transformed a 40-year-old immigration database—
the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, or “SAVE”—into a new 
tool for mass “voter verification” and benefits eligibility checks. The modified system 
(“Modified SAVE”) performs bulk searches of SSA data to check individuals’ U.S. 
citizenship status, even though the government admits this data is not a reliable 
indicator of current citizenship status. The government created the system despite 
internally acknowledging it violated federal privacy laws and risked misidentifying 
eligible voters as non-citizens. And the flawed system has resulted in error rates as 
high as 81% in some localities. Among the American citizens caught in the fallout are 
Respondents’ members, whose privacy and voting rights were violated and remain 
imperiled by Modified SAVE.
The court of appeals correctly refused to stay the district court’s summary 
judgment order vacating the government’s 2025 SAVE modifications pending appeal, 
and this Court should do the same. The government cannot meet its heavy burden to 
obtain this “extraordinary” relief. App.104a.

2
The government is not likely to succeed on the merits. Respondents have 
standing because Modified SAVE inflicts cognizable injuries on their members’ 
voting, privacy, and reputational interests. The government forfeited key arguments 
below. And the SAVE modifications exceeded Applicants’ statutory authority and 
violated the Social Security Act, Privacy Act, and Administrative Procedure Act. 
Applicants’ merits arguments hinge on a flawed, newly advanced reading of a 
30-year-old statute, 8 U.S.C. § 1373. That reading misconstrues prohibitory text in 
§ 1373(a) and § 1373(b) (“may not prohibit, or in any way restrict”) as an affirmative 
grant of authority to consolidate and disclose millions of Americans’ protected 
information. And it misconstrues DHS’s duty to “respond” to a citizenship inquiry 
under § 1373(c) as impliedly “overrid[ing]” all preexisting statutory restrictions on 
disclosure, including the Social Security Act and Privacy Act. App.22-23. 
The government’s boundless reading of § 1373 defies normal rules of statutory 
construction and the Executive’s own longstanding interpretation of the statute. 
Accepting it would give DHS unlimited power to vacuum up millions of Americans’ 
sensitive information from SSA (or any other agency) and disclose it in bulk to states 
however it wants. Surely if Congress meant to confer that extraordinary power, it 
would have done so clearly and expressly. It did not. Meanwhile, several bills that 
would expressly authorize the SAVE modifications have failed in Congress. Modified 
SAVE thus has “conveniently” enabled DHS and SSA to “‘enact a program’ that 
Congress has chosen not to enact itself.” Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477, 503 (2023).
Neither the government nor the public will be harmed by continuing to limit 
SAVE to its pre-2025 functionality pending appeal, the status quo since June 22. 
Agencies remain free to use SAVE for individualized citizenship checks as they did 
for decades prior to 2025. And states remain free to use their own robust voter 
registration and list-maintenance processes to ensure the integrity of their voter rolls.
The government also lacks a substantial interest in operating a citizenship

3
database it admits is error-prone and unreliable. Though the government touts 
SAVE’s “millions” of “verification[s],” App.4, it omits the number of eligible voters
whose citizenship SAVE has inaccurately called into question, and who consequently 
have been erroneously purged from voter rolls or forced to reverify their citizenship, 
which includes Respondents’ members. “[N]othing in this preliminary stay posture 
necessarily calls for allocating the risk of error to citizens eligible to vote who may be 
burdened by inaccurate modified-SAVE results rather than to states temporarily 
unable to use modified SAVE’s new functionality.” App.118a.
This case is an especially poor candidate for emergency relief for three 
additional reasons. First, the government seeks review not of an order granting 
preliminary relief, but of a summary judgment decision following cross-dispositive 
motions based on a voluminous administrative record. The Court should not grant 
“emergency relief in a fact-intensive and highly technical case without fully engaging 
with both the relevant law and the voluminous record.” Ohio v. EPA, 603 U.S. 279, 
300 (2024) (Barrett, J., dissenting). Second, this case involves arguments that all 
judges below (including the dissenting judge) found that the government forfeited. 
See App.104a, 142a. This Court “‘normally declines to entertain’ arguments ‘forfeited’ 
by the parties,” Ohio, 603 U.S. at 298-99, and doing so at the emergency stay stage 
would be “highly unusual” since it would require the Court “to doubly exercise 
discretion in [the government’s] favor,” App.120a, 114a. Finally, the court of appeals
expedited the appeal in denying a stay, App.103a, and noted a “subsequent merits 
panel remains free to decide” whether to excuse the government’s forfeiture, 
App.120a, further undercutting the need for this Court’s immediate intervention. 
The application for a stay should be denied.1
1 “App.” refers to the stay application. “Dkt.” refers to district court docket entries.
The administrative record was docketed in the district court at Dkt.110, and cited 
excerpts (e.g., DHS-AR-XXX) are included in the attached supplemental appendix.

4
STATEMENT
I. Statutory Background
A. The Social Security Act of 1935
The Social Security Act of 1935 created financial assistance benefit programs 
for millions of Americans. Pub. L. No. 74-271, 49 Stat. 620 (codified at 42 U.S.C. § 301 
et seq.). Privacy was central to Social Security from the start. The Social Security 
Board’s first regulation prohibited any “member, officer, or employee of the Board” 
from disclosing “any record . . . or any information acquired therefrom . . . pertaining 
to any person.” Disclosure of Official Records & Information, 2 Fed. Reg. 1256, 1256 
(June 18, 1937). In 1939, Congress codified that prohibition in the Social Security Act. 
See Social Security Act Amendments of 1939, Pub. L. No. 76-379, title VIII, § 1106, 
53 Stat. 1360, 1398. Today, the Act prohibits SSA’s “disclosure . . . of any file, record, 
report, or other paper, or any information . . . except as . . . agency . . . regulations 
prescribe and except as otherwise provided by Federal law.” 42 U.S.C. § 1306(a). 
Another provision prohibits any “officer or employee of the United States” from 
disclosing the “[s]ocial security account numbers and related records that are 
obtained or maintained . . . pursuant to any provision of law enacted on or after 
October 1, 1990.” 42 U.S.C. §§ 405(c)(2)(C)(viii)(I), (III). A “related record” is “any 
record, list, or compilation that indicates, directly or indirectly, the identity of any 
individual with respect to whom a social security account number or a request for a 
social security account number is maintained.” Id. § 405(c)(2)(C)(viii)(IV). 
SSA’s policy manual recognizes that SSA does “not have the legal authority to 
disclose information about U.S. citizens to DHS,” and that “[i]f DHS requests 
information and [SSA] determine[s] the information pertains to both U.S. citizens 
and aliens, only information about the aliens can be disclosed.” SSA Program 
Operation Manual System (“POMS”), GN 03325.002 Disclosure and Verification of 
Social Security Numbers (SSN) Without Consent (2023), https://perma.cc/PE44-2QBK

5
(“SSA Disclosure Policy”); accord SSA POMS, GN 03313.095 Disclosure to the 
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) (2025), https://perma.cc/NZR7-MVB7.
B. The Privacy Act of 1974
The Privacy Act of 1974 established “safeguards for an individual against an 
invasion of personal privacy.” Pub. L. No. 93-579, § 2(b)(4), 88 Stat. 1896, 1896 
(codified at 5 U.S.C. § 552a note). The Act “was passed largely out of concern over ‘the 
impact of computer data banks on individual privacy.’” DOJ v. Reps. Comm. for 
Freedom of the Press, 489 U.S. 749, 766 (1989) (quoting H.R. Rep. No. 93–1416, at 7 
(1974)); see also Londrigan v. FBI, 670 F.2d 1164, 1169 (D.C. Cir. 1981) (statute was 
enacted amid “growing awareness that governmental agencies were accumulating an 
ever-expanding stockpile of information about private individuals that was readily 
susceptible to both misuse and the perpetuation of inaccuracies that the citizen would 
never know of, let alone have an opportunity to rebut or correct”); App.4a-7a 
(providing statutory background). Thus, the Act’s substantive and procedural 
safeguards prevent the government from creating “centralized Federal information 
systems” or “interagency computer data banks” that consolidate Americans’ sensitive 
information across agencies in ways that could endanger our fundamental rights. S. 
Comm. on Gov’t Operations and H.R. Comm. on Gov’t Operations, 94th Cong., Source 
Book on Privacy 168, 217, 885 (1976), https://perma.cc/9W9F-R5ZL.
Pertinent here, the Privacy Act prohibits “an agency” from “disclos[ing] a 
record to another agency” or other entity “without the written consent of the person 
to whom the record pertains,” subject to “certain exceptions.” FAA v. Cooper, 566 U.S. 
284, 289 n.2 (2012) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b)). One such exception is for a properly 
noticed “routine use,” 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b)(3), defined as a use “for a purpose which is 
compatible with the purpose for which [a record] was collected,” id. § 552a(a)(7).
The Act also imposes strict notice-and-comment requirements. When agencies 
“establish[] or revis[e]” any “system of records,” they must “publish in the Federal

6
Register . . . a notice,” id. § 552a(e)(4)—called a System of Records Notice (“SORN”)—
disclosing the system’s contents, functions, uses, and procedures for individuals to 
access and correct records about themselves. Id. Agencies must publish a SORN at 
least 30 days before “any new use or intended use of the information in the system, 
and provide an opportunity for interested persons to submit written data, views, or 
arguments.” Id. § 552a(e)(11). 
Contemporaneous Privacy Act guidelines issued by the Office of Management 
and Budget (“OMB”) pursuant to a statutory delegation, see 5 U.S.C. § 552a(v)(1), 
confirm that the Act requires a meaningful opportunity for notice and comment, with 
a public “explanation of the routine uses and any changes made or not made as a 
result of the public comment.” Privacy Act Implementation: Guidelines and 
Responsibilities, 40 Fed. Reg. 28948, 28966 (July 9, 1975), https://perma.cc/776J4L46; accord OMB Circular No. A-108, Federal Agency Responsibilities for Review, 
Reporting, and Publication under the Privacy Act, at 7 & 12 (2016), 
https://perma.cc/N9QK-SDLE. 
II. Factual Background
A. The SAVE System and its 2025 Modifications
“Congress created SAVE in 1986, directing DHS’s predecessor to establish an 
automated means of verifying the immigration status of noncitizens applying for 
certain public benefits.” App.105a (citing Immigration Reform and Control Act of 
1986, Pub. L. No. 99-603, § 121(c)(1), 100 Stat. 3359, 3391 (codified at 42 U.S.C. 
§ 1320b-7(d)). Consistent with SAVE’s statutory purpose of verifying whether “aliens” 
are eligible for government “benefits,” 42 U.S.C. § 1320b-7(d), for “nearly four 
decades, SAVE principally searched DHS’s own immigration records,” App.105a. The 
system did not incorporate records on U.S.-born citizens (as DHS would have no 
immigration records on them), did not allow searches using Social Security numbers

7
or access SSA databases, and only allowed queries of one person at a time. Id.2
That changed in 2025, when the President issued an Executive Order directing 
DHS to provide states “access to appropriate systems for verifying the citizenship or 
immigration status of individuals registering to vote or who are already registered.” 
Exec. Order No. 14248, § 2(b)(i), 90 Fed. Reg. 14005, 14006 (Mar. 25, 2025). The order 
also directed SSA to make its Social Security Number Verification Service, Death 
Master File, and other relevant federal databases available for that purpose. Id.
§ 3(a), 90 Fed. Reg. at 14007.
Soon thereafter, DHS modified SAVE “in three principal respects: (i) it 
connected SAVE to SSA records and permitted searches using full or partial SSNs; 
(ii) that connection allowed SAVE to return information about persons—including 
many U.S.-born citizens—who had no DHS immigration records; and (iii) the system 
permitted bulk queries.” App.106a; accord App.133a (Katsas, J., dissenting).3 
As authority for these modifications, DHS’s and SSA’s 2025 agreement for 
Modified SAVE invoked a 30-year-old statute, 8 U.S.C. § 1373, which the agencies 
had never previously construed to permit such data sharing. DHS-AR-421. Prior to 
making the modifications, neither agency published modified SORNs for the relevant 
systems of records “or otherwise provided an opportunity for the public to comment”
as required by the Privacy Act. App.12a. 
B. The Modified SAVE Process
Modified SAVE results in federal agencies disclosing, and SAVE users 
2 Also, before 2025, DHS recognized SAVE as a Privacy Act “system of records,” issued 
SORNs, and conducted notice and comment before making changes to the system. 
See App.10a (citing eight SAVE SORNs issued between 2001 and 2020).
3 Modified SAVE links directly to SSA’s Master Files (known as NUMIDENT), a 
highly sensitive system of records with information on over 300 million U.S. citizens, 
including SSNs, other identifying numbers, names, dates and places of birth, 
citizenship indicators, and death records. See SSA-AR-238; 90 Fed. Reg. 10025, 10026 
(Feb. 20, 2025).

8
accessing, millions of Americans’ sensitive information through a four-step process. 
First, a SAVE user (e.g., a state election official) uploads into a web interface 
a spreadsheet with various data elements (first and last name, date of birth, a full or 
partial SSN, and the reason for verification) for up to millions of individuals. 
App.106a.
Second, DHS discloses these data elements to SSA, which uses it to search the 
SSA Master Files. Id.
Third, SSA “generates separate true-or-false match indicators for the SSN, 
name, and date of birth for each person.” Id. SSA sends DHS “match results, as well 
as yes-or-no indicators capturing whether queried individuals are citizens, deceased, 
or foreign-born, and other data fields that indicate state or country of birth and alien 
registration number if applicable and available.” Id. And if the user initially “provided 
only a partial SSN and SSA nonetheless identified a match in its own records, SSA 
shares the associated full (nine-digit) SSN with DHS for DHS’s own records.” Id. 
Fourth, Modified SAVE discloses results to the SAVE user. “For each person 
encompassed by the query, the SAVE results report the name, SSN, date of birth, and 
other identifying information contained in the request, alongside search results. The 
search results may include an indicator of citizenship or immigration status, an 
indicator capturing whether the individual is deceased, and descriptions of errors 
generated by the search process.” App.107a. These results are disclosed to the end 
user in a “person-specific . . . SAVE case response.” App.125a; see USCIS, FOIA 
Release, Control No. COW2025005720 (June 26, 2026), https://perma.cc/23F9-9W8N
(sample SAVE responses).
Under DHS’s standard SAVE user agreement, if Modified SAVE returns an 
inconclusive or non-U.S. citizen response, DHS instructs SAVE users that they must
“‘contact the [individual] to obtain proof of U.S. citizenship.’” App.7 (quoting DHSAR-762); see also App.13, 107a; DHS-AR-449. Absent action by that individual, DHS’s

9
agreement contemplates their voter registration can be canceled. DHS-AR-1526.
C. The Government Admits Modified SAVE’s Citizenship Data Is 
Incomplete and Unreliable
DHS knew when it modified SAVE that the changes violated the Privacy Act 
and that, due to “shortfalls in data accuracy,” the modified system could not reliably 
confirm citizenship for citizens born outside the United States (e.g., naturalized, 
derived, and acquired citizens).4 See App.111a; DHS-AR-260, -277, -302, -319 (DHS 
“Privacy Threshold Analysis” documents from July and September 2025 finding that 
SAVE modifications were “not in compliance” with the Privacy Act, and that 
“[s]hortfalls in data accuracy could cause incomplete or false results”); DHS-AR-240 
(DHS “Privacy Impact Assessment” warning Modified SAVE “may share inaccurate 
information with registered agencies” and “may produce inaccurate results”).
Specifically, Modified SAVE incorporates SSA citizenship data that only 
reflects a person’s citizenship status when they applied for an SSN; that status does 
not automatically update if the person later naturalizes, nor must the individual 
report a change in their citizenship status unless applying for SSA benefits. See SSAAR-103, -44. Thus, a naturalized citizen who applied for a Social Security card or 
otherwise interacted with SSA before naturalization may be incorrectly identified as 
a non-citizen in SSA records. See SSA-AR-44 (“[C]itizenship information in SSA’s 
records might not be current.”); SSA-AR-103 (SSA “citizenship information is 
accurate for SSA’s program purposes” only; “if used later for other purposes, it may 
not be current”). Similarly, if an acquired or derived citizen has not obtained a 
“certificate of United States citizenship” from DHS—which “frequently” is the case, 
4 Acquired citizenship is “[c]itizenship conferred at birth on children born abroad to 
a U.S. citizen parent(s).” USCIS, Acquired citizenship, Glossary of Terms, 
https://perma.cc/8AB4-9LAX. Derived citizenship is “[c]itizenship conveyed to 
children through the naturalization of their parents or, under certain circumstances, 
to foreign-born children adopted by U.S. citizen parents.” USCIS, Derivative 
citizenship, Glossary of Terms, https://perma.cc/7SXE-ZTYT.

10
DHS-AR-259—then “SAVE may not be able to confirm [that individual’s] U.S. 
citizenship.” DHS-AR-1525; accord DHS-AR-1529; DHS-AR-496 n.2. 
While the government touts the “millions” of citizenship “verification[s]” 
Modified SAVE has allegedly enabled, see App.4, it has never disclosed Modified 
SAVE’s error rate, including the number of Americans whose U.S. citizenship 
Modified SAVE failed to confirm, whose status it has misrepresented, and who 
consequently have been forced to reverify their citizenship to retain their voter 
registration or obtain government benefits.
The record shows that Modified SAVE has high rates of erroneous non-citizen 
or non-verification responses (either of which triggers DHS’s directive that voters 
provide proof of citizenship, see App.7). In Travis County, Texas, “‘twenty-five percent 
of the non-citizen matches’ in that county were individuals who had already proven 
citizenship in the United States.” App.35a. The public record reflects that at least 
81% of Modified SAVE’s responses to St. Louis County, Missouri were erroneous, with 
other jurisdictions across the country receiving similarly unreliable SAVE 
responses.5 Respondents’ members are among the victims of Modified SAVE’s stale 
and faulty citizenship data. See infra Argument § I.A.
D. The SAVE Modifications Were Unprecedented
By all accounts, the 2025 SAVE modifications were transformative and 
unprecedented. See App.34-37; App.133a, 136a, 151a-152a (Katsas, J., dissenting). 
As noted, Congress established SAVE to help verify non-citizens’ eligibility for 
government benefits. Consistent with that limited statutory purpose, SAVE 
previously enabled only individualized searches of non-citizens and “certain 
5 See Jen Fifield & Zach Despart, “Not Ready for Prime Time.” A Federal Tool to Check 
Voter Citizenship Keeps Making Mistakes, ProPublica & Texas Tribune (Feb. 13, 
2026), https://perma.cc/PR4Q-67NR; Judd Legum & Rebecca Crosby, The Federal 
Database That Could Upend the Midterm Elections, Mother Jones (Apr. 9, 2026), 
https://perma.cc/8YXC-WU7U.

11
naturalized and derived U.S. citizens” and could not verify U.S. born citizens “under 
any circumstances.” USCIS, Voter Registration and Voter List Maintenance Fact 
Sheet (Jan. 24, 2025), https://perma.cc/QW29-JZK8. By expanding SAVE beyond its 
statutory design to incorporate SSA’s Master Files and enable bulk searches of U.S.-
born citizens, DHS enlarged the population of Americans whose sensitive personal 
information SAVE accesses by over 1,000%—from about 27 million foreign-born 
citizens to more than 300 million Americans.6 Never before has a government agency 
created an inter-agency citizenship database centralizing Americans’ sensitive 
personal information at the scale and scope of Modified SAVE.
III. Procedural Background
Respondents are organizations whose members had their personal information 
disclosed without their consent and/or were wrongfully identified as non-citizens 
because of Modified SAVE. App.2a-3a. Some were purged from voter rolls as a result. 
App.33a. Respondents filed suit in September 2025 to challenge Modified SAVE as 
substantively and procedurally unlawful, Dkt.1, and moved for preliminary relief, 
Dkt.16. While that motion was pending, DHS and SSA belatedly published updated 
SORNs for Modified SAVE. App.13a. Although the SORNs “solicited comments from 
the public,” they also provided Modified SAVE “would be effective immediately (i.e., 
before the public could submit comments).” App.13a.
After DHS and SSA produced voluminous administrative records and the 
6 See U.S. Census Bureau, Nativity and Citizenship Status in the United States, 
https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2023.B05001?q=B05001 (accessed Feb. 23, 
2026) (estimating about 25 million naturalized citizens in United States); Sarah 
Miller, Estimates of the Lawful Permanent Resident Population in the United States 
and the Subpopulation Eligible to Naturalize: 2024 and Revised 2023, Office of 
Homeland Sec’y Statistics, at 3 (Sept. 2024), https://perma.cc/E4TP-6FWX 
(estimating some 2 million lawful permanent residents who derived citizenship from 
a parent since 1980); SSA-AR-238 (SSA Master Files include information on “easily 
over 300 million” Americans).

12
parties engaged in comprehensive summary judgment briefing, the court entered 
summary judgment for Respondents on multiple claims. App.1a. The court found that 
Respondents League of Women Voters (“LWV”) and League of Women Voters Texas 
(“LWVTX”) had associational standing based on their members’ privacy, 
reputational, voting, and procedural injuries. App.23a-40a.7 On the merits, the court 
held Modified SAVE and the associated SORNs “unlawful in several respects”: they 
violated the Social Security Act’s prohibition against “disclosure of Social Security 
numbers and other related SSA records,” substantive and procedural protections of 
the Privacy Act, and the APA. App.3a.8 The court also rejected the government’s 
claims about the impact of litigation in the Northern District of Florida between four 
plaintiff states and DHS (but not SSA), see Florida v. DHS, No. 24-cv-00509 (N.D. 
Fla.) (“Florida”), finding it lacked authority to enforce another court’s consent decree 
and, even if it could, “comity does not favor dismissing or abstaining in this 
circumstance.” App.72a.9 The court therefore “set[] aside and vacate[d] the 2025 
7 Because these “injuries suffice[d] to confer standing,” the court did not address 
Respondents’ organizational and informational standing. App.23a n.5. 
8 Because relief was “warranted on these [statutory] claims,” the court did not address 
Respondents’ constitutional claims. App.21a. 
9 In Florida—four months after DHS internally acknowledged its SAVE modifications 
were “not in compliance” with the Privacy Act, DHS-AR-319, -326, two months after 
Respondents filed this suit, and eleven days after the district court wrote it “doubt[ed] 
the lawfulness of the Government’s actions,” Dkt.55 at 1—four plaintiff states and 
DHS executed a consent decree purporting to require DHS to maintain Modified 
SAVE. After the district court here vacated the SAVE modifications, the Florida court 
granted the plaintiffs’ motion to enforce their consent agreement with DHS, ordering 
DHS to reinstate those states’ access to Modified SAVE despite the contrary vacatur 
order in this case, and despite the lack of adversarial proceedings in Florida over the 
lawfulness of Modified SAVE. Respondents LWV and EPIC intervened in Florida to 
appeal the district court’s enforcement order. See Florida v. League of Women Voters, 
No. 26-12533 (11th Cir.). That appeal is ongoing.

13
SAVE modified system and the related [SORNs].” App.3a; see also App.74a-77a.10
The government appealed and moved to stay the order pending appeal. 
Dkt.113; Dkt.116. The district court denied the stay motion. App.78a. It affirmed its 
prior conclusions, and it held that the government’s newly advanced arguments about 
the Social Security Act were unlikely to succeed because they were forfeited. App.81a. 
The court found that any injuries to the government were “minimal” and “selfinflicted,” App.90a, 92a, and that the Florida court “had no authority to make merits 
determinations about the legality of SAVE” in entering a consent decree, App.91a96a; accord App.119a.
The court of appeals also denied a stay. The court found Respondents’ members 
face “cognizable” voting injuries that are “sufficiently likely to establish their 
standing,” “fairly traceable” to Modified SAVE, and “redressable” by “setting [it] 
aside.” App.110a-112a. On the merits, the court found that the government forfeited 
“what are now its central arguments” under the Social Security Act, having first 
raised them in their post-judgment stay motion and declined the district court’s 
“express[]” invitation to “submit a post-judgment motion to excuse the forfeiture and 
receive full consideration of the late-raised arguments.” App.104a. The court also 
rejected the government’s claim of authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1373(c). App.120a-122a. 
Finally, the court concluded that the government failed to make “the requisite strong 
showing of a likelihood of success” even if its forfeiture were excused. App.122a-130a.
ARGUMENT
To obtain a stay pending appeal, the “applicant must show that it is likely to 
succeed on the merits of its appeal, that [this Court] would likely grant certiorari to 
review any decision to the contrary, that it will likely suffer irreparable harm in the

I. The Government is Unlikely to Succeed on the Merits
A. Respondents Have Standing
Respondents have associational standing on behalf of their members based on 
voting, privacy, and reputational injuries caused by Modified SAVE. The government 
is not likely to show otherwise.
Voting Injuries. Modified SAVE harms Respondents’ members’ voting rights, 
with its continued operation substantially increasing the risk of forced verification of 
citizenship, deregistration, and even disenfranchisement—as reflected in the opinion 
of every judge who addressed this issue below. See App.31a-38a (Sooknanan, J.); 
App.110a-112a (Srinivasan, C.J., and Wilkins, J.); cf. App.139a, 153a (Katsas, J., 
dissenting) (not disputing standing).
Because Modified SAVE discloses inaccurate citizenship data to SAVE users, 
Respondents’ members who are naturalized and derived citizens have been forced to 
provide documentary proof of citizenship to maintain their voter registrations, with 
some having their registrations wrongfully cancelled. See App.110a-112a. And 
similarly situated members across the country will face the same harms if the 
government is allowed to resume use of Modified SAVE. See id. These burdens on the 
fundamental right to vote, including the substantial risk of future burdens if Modified 
SAVE continues, easily establish standing. See Meese v. Keene, 481 U.S. 465, 475 
(1985) (“[T]he need to take . . . affirmative steps to avoid the risk of harm . . .
constitutes a cognizable injury.”); Gill v. Whitford, 585 U.S. 48, 65-66 (2018)

15
(“‘[V]oters who allege facts showing disadvantage to themselves as individuals have 
standing to sue’ to remedy that disadvantage.”); App.111a (“If a person needs to prove 
their citizenship to remain registered to vote or if they are removed from the 
registration rolls, they suffer a cognizable injury.”); App.32a-36a (citing cases).
The government disputes neither the facts underpinning these voting injuries, 
nor the injuries’ legal sufficiency. Instead, it focuses on traceability and redressability
by denying that its actions are responsible for Respondents’ members’ injuries. 
App.12-16. But the government misstates the law. “Article III ‘requires no more than 
de facto causality.’” Dep’t of Com. v. New York, 588 U.S. 752, 768 (2019). This Court 
has repeatedly recognized that a plaintiff has standing if “‘third parties will likely 
react’ to the government [action] ‘in predictable ways’ that will likely cause . . . the 
plaintiff’s injury.” Diamond Alt. Energy, LLC v. EPA, 606 U.S. 100, 112 (2025) 
(cleaned up). And even “‘a partial remedy’ satisfies the redressability requirement.” 
Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski, 592 U.S. 279, 291 (2021).
These standards are easily met here. As found below, “the undisputed record 
shows that the [Respondents’] members suffer th[e] injury [of burdens on their 
franchise] because SAVE records show that they are not United States citizens.” 
App.37a (cleaned up); see also App.110a-112a. “It is hardly surprising that additional 
voter verification and potential voter disenfranchisement is ‘the predictable effect of’ 
the federal government incorrectly informing a state that an individual may be 
ineligible to vote.” App.37a-38a; see also App.112a (“states’ response to an adverse 
SAVE result is not conjectural”). Indeed, the government concedes this is the 
intended effect: DHS agreements instruct users of Modified SAVE that they “must
contact the registrant or registered voter to obtain proof of U.S. citizenship” if SAVE 
cannot confirm citizenship. DHS-AR-762 (emphasis added); App.13. And the ordered 
relief redresses Respondents’ harms because it prospectively halts the unlawful use 
of Modified SAVE that has burdened, and would continue to burden, Respondents’

16
members’ voting rights. See App.112a. 
Article III does not require plaintiffs to eliminate all hypothetical alternative 
causes of a future injury. Contra App.13 (speculating that, even without Modified 
SAVE, states might hypothetically demand proof of citizenship or revoke 
registrations for other reasons). Respondents need only show that Modified SAVE is 
a “de facto caus[e]” of their injuries. Dep’t of Com., 588 U.S. at 768. Through 
unrebutted evidence, they have done exactly that. See App.37a; App.110a-112a.
Applicants incorrectly assert that the courts below “never found” Modified

Modified SAVE because it is “more accurate.” App.14. In reality, the courts below

App.110a-112a. These findings are based on the government’s own acknowledgment 
of “‘[s]hortfalls in data accuracy’ in SSA citizenship data” that “could produce 
‘incomplete or false results.’” App.111a (quoting DHS-AR-260, -302); see also supra
Statement § II.C.

an exact duplicate.” Id. at 433. The district court correctly concluded that both 
intrusion upon seclusion and breach of confidence provide such an analogue here.

basis for lawsuits in American courts. Id. at 425. The tort’s relevant elements are 
“intentional[]” intrusion, “physically or otherwise, upon the . . . private affairs or 
concerns” of another which “would be highly offensive to a reasonable person.”

even the subject’s knowledge that an intrusion has occurred. See id. cmt. b, illus. 1–
5; cmt. c, illus. 7; see also Am. Fed’n of State, Cnty. & Mun. Emps., AFL-CIO v. Soc. 
Sec. Admin., 172 F.4th 361, 370-71 (4th Cir. 2026) (en banc); contra App.17.
“Breach of confidence”—a tort with roots in equity—is also a traditionally 
recognized basis for a lawsuit. See, e.g., Corliss v. E.W. Walker Co., 64 F. 280 (D. Mass. 
1894) (recognizing “violation of confidence” as allowing equitable relief). “The 
equitable jurisdiction in cases of breach of confidence is ancient.” Coco v. A.N. Clark 
(Engineers) Ltd., [1968] F.S.R. 415, 419 (Ch.) (Eng.). Today recognized as a tort, 
“breach of confidence” is actionable where a person offers private information to a 
third party in confidence and the third party reveals that information. Jeffries v.

A person’s SSN and specific citizenship or immigration status are precisely the

Applicants rely on the forfeited argument that SAVE discloses only whether

see also App.127a (“There are sound reasons to think verification of that kind might

well amount to a ‘disclos[ure]’ of an SSN for purposes of § 405(c)(2)(C)(viii)(I)”); infra

public. Contra App.17. As explained above, intrusion upon seclusion requires no

This Court has noted that “[b]ecause the [Privacy] Act serves interests similar 
to those protected by defamation and privacy torts, there is good reason to infer that

has explained that “[i]n determining whether a harm is sufficiently concrete to qualify

added). Nothing in the IRCA authorizes using SAVE to verify individuals’ U.S.

2. The government chiefly relies on 8 U.S.C. § 1373, a section of the IIRIRA.
Section 1373 consists of three subsections—each of which addresses a discrete point,

and none of which support the government’s position. Section 1373(a) provides that,

that, “[n]otwithstanding any other provision of” law, “no person or agency may 
prohibit, or in any way restrict,” a government entity from sending, requesting, 
exchanging, or maintaining “information regarding the immigration status, lawful or 
unlawful, of any individual.” Id. § 1373(b). And § 1373(c) provides that DHS “shall 
respond to an inquiry by a . . . government agency, seeking to verify or ascertain the

The government mashes these discrete subsections together, construing the 
“notwithstanding” clauses of subsections (a) and (b) to apply to subsection (c) (even 
though it has no such clause), and insisting that § 1373 as a whole nullifies any 
provision of the U.S. Code that might restrict DHS’s acquisition and disclosure of 
information under § 1373, including the Social Security Act and Privacy Act. App.22-

the Executive’s own longstanding interpretation of the statute.
Start with § 1373(a) and § 1373(b). Those subsections use purely prohibitory 
language, stating government entities “may not prohibit, or in any way restrict” 
certain action. Prohibitory language such as “shall not” or “may not” is not “an 
affirmative grant of power.” See New England Power Co. v. New Hampshire, 455 U.S. 
331, 341 (1982). Nothing in § 1373(a) or § 1373(b) affirmatively empowers DHS and 
SSA to freely exchange data for purposes of verifying “citizen and immigration 
status,” despite the web of preexisting statutory restrictions on such inter-agency

27
disclosures. And the “Executive Branch interpretation . . . issued roughly 
contemporaneously with enactment of the statute” and “the longstanding ‘practice of 
the government’” since the IIRIRA’s enactment confirms as much. Loper Bright, 603 
U.S. at 386; see Relationship Between Illegal Immigr. Reform & Immigrant Resp. Act 
of 1996 & Statutory Requirement for Confidentiality of Census Info., 1999 WL 
34995963, *4-*6 (O.L.C. May 18, 1999) (recognizing that neither § 1373(a) nor 
§ 1373(b) “clearly invest[s]” agencies with “affirmative authority to disclose 
information in circumstances where they otherwise would be prohibited from doing 
so by a federal statute”); supra Statement § II.A.15
Nor does § 1373(c) authorize Modified SAVE. To start, § 1373(c) speaks solely 
to DHS’s obligations and confers no authority whatsoever on SSA. That point is 
dispositive here because, absent express authorization, the Social Security Act 
prohibits SSA from disclosing its records outside of the agency, see supra Argument 
§ I.B, and Modified SAVE cannot operate without SSA doing so, see supra Statement
§ II.B.
Even as to DHS, the court of appeals correctly held its “general duty to answer 
a citizenship inquiry under 8 U.S.C. § 1373(c) does not by itself authorize disclosure

government’s contrary position—that § 1373(c) “overrides” disclosure restrictions of

presumption that repeals by implication are disfavored and that Congress will

D. The SAVE Modifications Were Arbitrary and Capricious
The district court correctly held that the SAVE modifications were arbitrary 
and capricious because they violated the change-in-position doctrine. Under that 
doctrine, “[a]gencies are free to change their existing policies as long as they provide

31
a reasoned explanation for the change,” “display awareness that [they are] changing 
position,” and consider “serious reliance interests.” FDA v. Wages & White Lion Invs., 
604 U.S. 542, 568 (2025). “An agency may not, for example, depart from a prior policy 
sub silentio or simply disregard rules that are still on the books.” FCC v. Fox 
Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009). The duty to explain and consider 
reliance interests is particularly important when there have been “decades” of 
reliance on the prior policy. See Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 222
(2016). Review of these actions “is limited to ‘the grounds that the agency invoked 
when it took the action.’” DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal. (“Regents”), 591 U.S. 1, 
20 (2020). Post hoc rationalizations are “impermissible.” Id. at 21.
The government has conceded that the transformation of SAVE, from a 
targeted tool to search individuals using DHS-issued identifiers to one allowing bulk 
searches of every citizen’s SSA data, amounted to a change in position. App.62a. 
These changes were implemented in a way that made it impossible for 
Applicants to meet the APA’s reasoned decision-making requirements. The Privacy 
Act requires a thirty-day notice-and-comment period “prior to” a new routine use of 
SAVE taking effect, 5 U.S.C. § 552a(e)(11) (emphasis added), but Modified SAVE was 
effective in May 2025 and no notice was published until October 2025, over a month 
after the present litigation was filed. See DHS-AR-114 (published October 31, 2025); 
SSA-AR-206 (published November 12, 2025). Even once Applicants published the 
required notices, they maintained that Modified SAVE was already in effect before 
publication, would remain in effect through the comment period, and that the notices 
would be “effective upon publication,” rather than after any period of consideration of 
public comments. DHS-AR-115. Ultimately, the agencies received over 30,550 
comments on the published SORNs. Dkt.66-1 at 8. As the district court correctly 
found, this untimely comment period meant that Petitioners could not have 
considered reliance interests before changing their position. App.62a.

32
The government’s heavy emphasis on excusing its procedural missteps, see 
App.27-29, suggests they missed the import of the district court’s analysis—that 
comments received months after modified SAVE went into effect, and after the 
government had already committed to making the new SORNs effective, “could not 
provide a ‘reasoned explanation for the change’ that the Federal Defendants 
undertook.” App.63a (quoting Wages & White Lion Invs., 604 U.S. at 568). Whatever 
consideration the agency may have given to issues raised by commenters was 
inherently post hoc and inconsistent with the APA’s requirement of reasoned 
decision-making. Regents, 591 U.S. at 21. 
The government concedes that it did not consider reliance interests but argues 
there were none to consider. App.30. This assertion is wrong, and it serves as an 
independently sufficient reason why the SAVE modifications violated the APA. See
Regents, 591 U.S. at 30-33 (holding agency action arbitrary and capricious for not 
considering reliance interests even though the agency thought there were none).
As the district court found, and as evidenced by the over-30,000 comments 
received by DHS and SSA, there were significant reliance interests. “[P]ersons who 
had provided information to SSA” and who had “failed to update SSA data” had 
reliance interests. App.62a-63a. These individuals include naturalized, derived, and 
acquired U.S. citizens who did not update their citizenship status in SSA records 
because there is no legal requirement to do so and because SSA records had never 
before been used to check the citizenship of registered voters. See supra Statement 
§ II.C. The change in position meant these individuals were placed at risk of being 
purged from voter rolls, prevented from voting, referred for criminal prosecution, or 
denied public benefits. Applicants’ admitted failure to consider these reliance 
interests was arbitrary and capricious. 
E. The SAVE Modifications Violated the Privacy Act
APA cause of action. Congress did not immunize agency policies that violate

33
the Privacy Act from review under the APA. App.45a-49a; contra App.23-26. The APA 
requires federal courts to “hold unlawful and set aside agency action” that is “not in 
accordance with law.” 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). “Law” here “means, of course, any law.” 
FCC v. NextWave Personal Commc’ns, Inc., 537 U.S. 293, 300 (2003) (emphasis in 
original). This Court embeds § 706(2)(A)’s mandate in a “strong presumption that 
Congress intends judicial review of administrative action.” Bowen v. Mich. Acad. of 
Fam. Phys., 476 U.S. 667, 670 (1986).
While this Court has not conclusively affirmed the availability of APA review 
for Privacy Act violations, is has twice acknowledged that “injunctive relief under the 
Administrative Procedure Act (APA)” may be available to “deter[] violations of [the 
Privacy Act’s] substantive provisions” for which the Act lacks a cause of action.
Cooper, 566 U.S. at 303 n.12; see also Doe v. Chao, 540 U.S. 614, 619 n.1 (2004) (“[T]he 
general provisions for equitable relief within the Administrative Procedure Act” may
explain the “inattention” of the Privacy Act to the “standards of proof governing 
equitable relief.”).
The government contends that since the Privacy Act creates some remedies for 
some injuries, it must “impliedly forbid[]” judicial review of all other agency action 
that violates the Privacy Act. App.24 (quoting 5 U.S.C. § 702). But this sweeping 
assertion ignores this Court’s admonishment that “Congress rarely allows claims 
about agency action to escape effective judicial review.” Axon Enter., Inc. v. Fed. 
Trade Comm’n, 598 U.S. 175, 186 (2023). Where Congress restricts judicial review, 
this Court expects to find “clear and convincing evidence” of a “legislative intent” to 
do so. Abbott Labs. v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136, 141 (1967).
The Privacy Act’s internal remedial scheme only provides for injunctive relief 
in two narrow situations: to force an agency to amend an individual’s record, and to 
force an agency to disclose an individual’s records to them. 5 U.S.C. § 552a(g)(2), 
(g)(3). But the Privacy Act imposes myriad other requirements on agencies, such as

34
the Act’s notice and comment requirements, id. § 552a(e)(7); and general prohibitions 
on disclosure of personal records within and outside the government, id. § 552a(b), 
accumulating records monitoring individuals’ exercise of First Amendment rights, id.
§ 552a(e)(7), and creating cross-agency computer programs matching personal 
information across disparate systems, id. § 552a(o). 
Congress did not intend to effectively preclude judicial review of violations of 
those requirements, just because it created the two narrow injunctive remedies 
codified in § 552a(g). As this Court has noted, a narrow remedial scheme should 
typically be understood as “exclusive where it applies,” but not necessarily to displace 
“general judicial review” elsewhere. Axon, 598 U.S. at 186 (emphasis added). For this 
Court to conclude otherwise, as Applicants advance, would mean the only mechanism 
for judicial review of programs that systematically violate the Privacy Act is for each 
of the millions of impacted Americans to litigate claims for monetary damages.
This Court has recognized that the availability of a “naked money judgment” 
will not “always be an adequate substitute for prospective relief” such that it displaces
general judicial review. Bowen v. Massachusetts, 487 U.S. 879, 905 (1988). Further, 
“to demand that every potentially affected party” bring such claims is “impractical—
and an enormous waste of resources.” McLaughlin Chiropractic Assocs., Inc. v. 
McKesson Corp., 606 U.S. 146, 158 (2025) (concerning pre-enforcement challenges to 
Hobbs Act violations, noting it is “unrealistic” to expect “more than a fraction” of 
affected people to have the familiarity with the Federal Register needed to bring 
challenges).
Contemporaneous understanding and subsequent statutory amendments 
confirm Congress’s intent to maintain APA review for some Privacy Act violations. 
The Privacy Act required OMB to issue “guidelines and regulations” for the Act’s 
implementation. 5 U.S.C. § 552a(v). Those guidelines, which were “issued 
contemporaneously with the” Act and “have remained consistent over time,” Loper

35
Bright, 603 U.S. at 394, “recognized that the Privacy Act’s judicial review provisions 
would not preclude ‘judicial review under other provisions of the [APA].’” App.49a 
(quoting 40 Fed. Reg. 28948, 28968 (July 9, 1975)). Further, the district court 
correctly noted that subsequent amendments to the Privacy Act have expressly
limited judicial review for certain populations not at issue in this case, in exactly the 
way that the government argues should be implied for the Act as a whole. App.49a. 
“Where Congress includes particular language in one section of a statute but omits it 
in another section of the same Act, it is generally presumed that Congress acts 
intentionally and purposely in the disparate inclusion or exclusion.” City & Cnty. of 
S.F., 604 U.S. at 344.
The text, structure, and contemporaneous and subsequent history of the 
Privacy Act do not make it likely that the government will supply a “persuasive 
reason to believe that Congress intended to preclude” injunctive relief for agency 
actions that violate the Privacy Act’s other requirements. McLaughlin, 606 U.S. at 
155-56 (cleaned up).
Violations of the Privacy Act’s Disclosure Restrictions. The district 
court correctly held Modified SAVE violated the Privacy Act’s restrictions on 
disclosure. See App.50a-56a; 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b). The government invokes just one 
exception to the Act’s general ban on disclosure without consent: the exception for 
disclosures pursuant to a “routine use.” App.26. That exception requires disclosures 
to be “both (i) for a purpose which is compatible with the purpose for which it was 
collected and (ii) within the scope of a routine use notice published by the agency.” 
App.50a (cleaned up) (quoting Ames v. DHS, 861 F.3d 238, 240 (D.C. Cir. 2017)); see
5 U.S.C. § 552a(a)(7). The compatibility requirement is not met here because the SSA 
records disclosed through Modified SAVE were “collected . . . for purposes concerning 
work authorization and eligibility for SSA benefits,” which does not have “any nexus 
to state governments’ voter verification efforts.” App.51a, 54a.

36
Regarding SSA’s disclosure of SSNs, the government adopts far too general a 
test to determine the “purpose” of that data’s collection—ignoring the limited ways in 
which SSNs are used when “‘keep[ing] track’ of” and “‘matching’” people. App.26. At
Applicants’ high level of abstraction, nearly any disclosure of SSA data could be called 
“routine.” But SSA creates and collects SSNs to keep track of and match future and 
current beneficiaries. The unabridged language from the government’s sole case, 
Bowen v. Roy, 476 U.S. 693, 710-711 (1986), proves this point: this Court observed 
that SSNs are used “to keep track of persons no longer entitled to receive food stamps
because of past fraud or abuses of the program,” and for matching “federal employee 
files against AFDC and Medicaid files to determine instances of Government 
employees receiving welfare benefits improperly.” Id. at 710 (emphasis added). SSNs 
are not collected for any voting-related purpose. Nor is receipt of benefits—which the 
political branches can extend or withdraw as they see fit, see Califano v. Aznavorian, 
439 U.S. 170, 174 (1978)—comparable to voting, a “right” that is “fundamental,” Bush 
v. Gore, 531 U.S. 98, 104 (2000). “Under any reasonable formulation of the 
compatibility test,” Ames, 861 F.3d at 240, n.1, the routine-use exception does not 
apply to disclosure of SSA citizenship data and SSNs through Modified SAVE. 
The government also ignores that SSA is not just disclosing SSNs through 
Modified SAVE; it is also disclosing the citizenship data it collects. See supra 
Statement § II.B. Again, SSA does not collect citizenship data for identification 
purposes; it collects the information “for purposes concerning work authorization and 
eligibility for SSA benefits.” App.51a. And SSA explicitly warns that its “‘citizenship 
information is accurate for SSA’s program purposes’ only—‘if used later for other 
purposes, it may not be current.’” App.51a (quoting SSA-AR-103). 
Violations of the Privacy Act’s Procedural Requirements. The district 
court correctly held that the SAVE modifications violated the Privacy Act’s 
procedural requirements. See App.58a-63a. As explained, agencies must both publish

37
a modified SORN 30 days before beginning a new routine use and meaningfully 
consider public comments received in response. See supra Statement § I.B. Applicants 
violated both requirements by making the SAVE modifications on a timeline that 
made it impossible to consider public comments before new routine uses went into 
effect, and then by failing to provide any explanation of “any changes made or not 
made as a result” of the more than 30,000 “public comment[s]” received. 40 Fed. Reg. 
at 28966; see supra Argument § I.D. 
Relying on Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter & Paul Home v. Pennsylvania, 
591 U.S. 657, 685 (2020), the government faults the district court for applying the 
“open-mindedness test” to the Privacy Act’s notice-and-comment requirements. 
App.28. Yet the government ignores the court’s exhaustive discussion of why Little 
Sisters “has little relevance here.” App.57a-60a. And the district court made clear its 
Privacy Act holding would be the same even if the government was “correct and [that] 
Little Sisters abrogated the D.C. Circuit’s use of the open-mindedness test” for 
purposes of the Privacy Act. App.60a.
II. The Remaining Factors Cut Sharply Against a Stay
Because “the Government has not shown that it is likely to prevail on the 
various legal arguments advanced in its stay application,” the Court should “start 
and stop with the first [stay] factor.” Trump, 146 S. Ct. at 2246; accord App.130a. But 
the remaining factors also weigh strongly against a stay. 
A. Applicants Will Suffer No Irreparable Harm
 The government is not irreparably harmed because—as it concedes—it is still 
able to provide SAVE verifications using the pre-2025 functionality it used for 
decades. App.34. The court of appeals noted that the government’s “principal 
operational harm from the denial of a stay” is that, without Modified SAVE, some 
citizenship and other verifications are, as the government described, “slower and

38
more cumbersome.” App.130a.17 While those constraints may require more work, 
“whatever its limitations, the preexisting SAVE program in operation for decades 
remains available to the states and to federal programs.” Id. Thus, any harm “stems 
from the unavailability of modified SAVE’s SSN- and bulk-search functionalities, not 
the loss of SAVE-based verification altogether.” App.130a-131a.
While the government claims “the district court’s order impairs the proper 
administration of federal elections,” App.34, there is no indication that Modified 
SAVE will meaningfully serve that interest. Modified SAVE’s unreliable citizenship 
data would impair the proper administration of elections by burdening the voting 
rights of lawful voters. And the main change made by Modified SAVE is that the 
system now sweeps in U.S.-born citizens, who indisputably have a right to vote.
The government also overstates the impact of the district court’s decision on 
the upcoming November 2026 election. As the court of appeals noted, App.131a, the 
National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) bars systematic voter-list maintenance 
within 90 days before a federal election. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A). In fact, the 
government itself argued, in opposing preliminary relief in the district court, that this 
90-day limitation precluded use of Modified SAVE for systematic voter-list
maintenance. See App.131a; Dkt.37 at 35-36. And as the court of appeals noted, “[b]y 
the time the government sought a stay pending appeal in this court, that limitation 
was already operative in several states and soon would be in many more,” 
undercutting any claim of harm. App.131a. Thus, it is “federal law itself—in the form 
of the NVRA—which constrains the principal election-related use of modified SAVE 
during the relevant period” and “[d]enying a stay thus does not deprive the 
government or the states of an otherwise available opportunity to undertake 
17 The court of appeals did not reach the factors of irreparable harm and balance of 
the equities, finding no likelihood of success on appeal, but noted several persuasive 
considerations that would inform that inquiry. App.130a-132a.

39
systematic voter-list maintenance while ordinary appellate review proceeds.” 
App.130a-131a. And, in any event, individualized searches in support of 
individualized voter eligibility determinations can still be run on the pre-2025 SAVE 
system, which remains available and would not violate the NVRA’s 90-day cut-off for 
systematic voter removal programs. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
The government’s remaining arguments are equally unpersuasive and 
unsupported by the record. The government argues that the order causes harm “[b]y 
preventing DHS from updating its own records with more current citizenship and 
immigration information held by SSA.” App.36. But SSA has made clear it does not 
maintain “current” citizenship data and “is not the custodian of U.S. citizenship 
records,” SSA-AR-44 (emphasis added), so it cannot be true that it has “more current 
citizenship and immigration information” than DHS, the agency that administers
immigration and citizenship laws. Nor does the cost of maintaining both versions of 
SAVE establish irreparable harm. As the district court found, this argument is 
factually unsupported, App.89a n.6, and nothing in its vacatur order requires
maintenance of Modified SAVE or any parallel systems of records. To the extent that
the government is voluntarily making that choice, “[s]uch self-imposed costs are not 
properly the subject of inquiry on a motion for stay.” Dep’t of Educ. v. California, 604 
U.S. 650, 652 (2025).
B. The Balance of Equities and Public Interest Favor Denying a 
Stay
The balance of the equities likewise supports denying the requested stay. See 
App.89a-99a. The public interest is best served by allowing the district court’s 
judgment to remain in effect, pending the appeal process, because it will protect 
millions of Americans’ privacy and voting rights. As the district court found and 
Applicants do not contest, Modified SAVE is riddled with inaccuracies. See App.69a, 
90a, 111a. And Applicants’ desire to expand the use of Modified SAVE risks

40
broadening the harms that erroneously flagged American citizens have already 
experienced. See App.32a-35a. With a major federal election 49 days away and many 
states’ voter registration deadlines fast approaching in the first week of October, 
erroneously identifying and removing voters based on indication of non-citizenship in 
stale, unreliable SAVE data would cause substantial harm to the rights of 
naturalized and derived citizen voters, including Respondents’ members. 
Moreover, the privacy interests Applicants dismiss as insufficiently “concrete,” 
App.16, are precisely the same interests that Congress already weighed in passing 
the Social Security Act and Privacy Act, “recognizing that the statutory protections 
might lead to decreased government efficiency.” App.90a. Courts should not “reject 
the balance that Congress has struck” among competing policy concerns. United 
States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers’ Co-op., 532 U.S. 483, 497 (2001).
Finally, for all practical purposes, the status quo was altered by the district 
court on June 22. Modified SAVE has been vacated for nearly three months, and the 
November general election is already underway. Reinstating Modified SAVE now 
would needlessly introduce confusion and administrative burdens amid an ongoing 
election cycle.18
On balance, the equities strongly favor denial of a stay.
CONCLUSION
The application for a stay should be denied.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
I. Background 
Congress mandated that the 
Immigration and Naturalization Service, 
as a precursor to the Department of 
Homeland Security (DHS) United States 
Citizenship and Immigration Services 
(USCIS), establish a system to verify the 
immigration status of individuals 
seeking government benefits. Authority 
for having a system for verification of 
citizenship and immigration status of 
individuals seeking government benefits 
can be found in the Immigration Reform 
and Control Act of 1986 (IRCA), Public 
Law (Pub. L.) 99–603; the Personal 
Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA), 
Public Law 104–193, 110 Stat. 2168; 
Title IV, Subtitle A, of the Illegal 
Immigration Reform and Immigrant 
Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA), 
Public Law 104–208, 110 Stat. 3009; and 
the Real ID Act of 2005, Public Law 
109–13. Based on these authorities and 
in accordance with the Privacy Act of 
1974, 5 U.S.C. 552a, DHS USCIS 
proposes to establish a new DHS system 
of records titled ‘‘DHS/USCIS–004 
Systematic Alien Verification for 
Entitlements Program System of 
Records.’’ 
USCIS Verification Division 
administers the Systematic Alien 
Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) 
Program, a fee-based intergovernmental 
initiative designed to help Federal, 
state, tribal, and local government 
agencies check immigration status when 
granting benefits, licenses, and other 
lawful purposes. SAVE is supported by 
and uses information derived from 
individuals, partner agencies, the 
Verification Information System (VIS) 
and other DHS, Department of State, 
and Department of Justice systems. 
The REAL ID Act of 2005, Public Law 
109–13, 119 Stat. 231, 302 (2005) 
(codified at 49 U.S.C. 30301 note) 
requires all state Departments of Motor 
Vehicles (DMV) to utilize the USCIS 
SAVE program to verify the legal 
immigration status of applicants for 
driver’s licenses, driver’s permits, and 
state-issued identification cards. 
Congress delayed the initial 
implementation date from May 2008 
until December 2009. DMVs access 
SAVE through the American 
Association of Motor Vehicle 
Administrators Network (AAMVAnet) 
or via Internet access using Web 3 or 
Web Services, which is a support 
service that allows SAVE customer 
agencies to access VIS information 
through a software interface. 
Previously, USCIS documented the 
SAVE and E-Verify Programs in the VIS 
Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) and 
System of Records Notice (SORN). VIS 
was and continues to be the underlying 
technology of both systems. In order to 
assist the public in better understanding 
the two programs, USCIS has issued a 
separate E-Verify SORN and, with this 
publication, is updating the original VIS 
SORN with this updated SORN. SAVE 
is described in previous SORNs, most 
recently in the VIS SORN (73 FR 75445, 
December 11, 2008). 
SAVE Usage Overview 
The SAVE Program was originally 
limited to immigration status 
verification for eligibility 
determinations of any public benefit, 
license, or credential—the benefit or 
‘‘entitlement’’ referred to in the name of 
the program. However, over time the 
scope of SAVE has grown to include the 
implementation of Section 642(c) of 
IIRIRA, which obligates USCIS to 
respond to inquiries ‘‘by a federal, state, 
or local government agency seeking to 
verify or ascertain the citizenship or 
immigration status of any individual 
within the jurisdiction of the agency for 
any purpose authorized by law.’’ This 
expansion was highlighted in previous 
versions of the SAVE Privacy Impact 
Assessment (PIA). 
Accordingly, to the extent that a 
Federal, state, or local government 
entity has the legal authority to verify 
immigration status, SAVE, as an access 
method to USCIS systems, is authorized 
to respond to the request. Specifically, 
in addition to verifications for purposes 
of granting government benefits, this 
includes verification for purposes of 
background investigations for 
individuals, and cohabitants of the 
individuals undergoing background 
investigations. 
Government agencies input 
biographic information into SAVE for 
status determinations. If SAVE has a 
record pertaining to the individual, the 
government agency automatically 
receives limited biographic information 
on the citizenship and immigration 
status of the individual. If SAVE does

II. Privacy Act 
The Privacy Act embodies fair 
information practice principles in a 
statutory framework governing the 
means by which the U.S. Government 
collects, maintains, uses, and 
disseminates individuals’ records. The 
Privacy Act applies to information that 
is maintained in a ‘‘system of records.’’ 
A ‘‘system of records’’ is a group of any 
records under the control of an agency 
for which information is retrieved by 
the name of an individual or by some 
identifying number, symbol, or other 
identifying particular assigned to the 
individual. In the Privacy Act, an 
individual is defined to encompass U.S. 
citizens and lawful permanent 
residents. As a matter of policy, DHS 
extends administrative Privacy Act 
protections to all individuals where 
systems of records maintain information 
on U.S. citizens, lawful permanent 
residents, and visitors. Below is the 
description of the DHS/USCIS–004 
Systematic Alien Verification for 
Entitlements Program System of 
Records. 
In accordance with 5 U.S.C. 552a(r), 
DHS has provided a report of this 
system of records to the Office of 
Management and Budget and to 
Congress.

AUTHORITY FOR MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM: 
Authority for having a system for 
verification of immigration status is 
found in IRCA, Public Law 99–603, 100 
Stat. 3359; PRWORA, Public Law 104– 
193, 110 Stat. 2105; Title IV, Subtitle A, 
of IIRIRA, Public Law 104–208, 110 
Stat. 3009; and the REAL ID Act of 2005, 
Public Law 109–13, 119 Stat. 231. 
PURPOSE(S): 
The purpose of the SAVE Program is 
to provide a fee-based 
intergovernmental service, which assists 
Federal, state, Tribal, or local 
government agencies, or contractors 
acting on the agency’s behalf and 
licensing bureaus confirm immigration 
status information, to the extent that 
such disclosure is necessary to enable 
these agencies to make decisions related 
to: (1) Determining of eligibility for a 
Federal, state, or local public benefit; (2) 
issuing a license or grant; (3) issuing a 
government credential; (4) conducting a 
background investigation; or (5) any 
other lawful purpose. 
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE
SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND
THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES: 
In addition to those disclosures 
generally permitted under 5 U.S.C. 
552a(b) of the Privacy Act, all or a 
portion of the records or information 
contained in this system may be 
disclosed outside DHS as a routine use 
pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 552a(b)(3) as 
follows: 
A. To the Department of Justice (DOJ), 
including U.S. Attorney Offices, or other 
Federal agencies conducting litigation 
or in proceedings before any court, 
adjudicative or administrative body, 
when it is necessary to the litigation and 
one of the following is a party to the 
litigation or has an interest in such 
litigation: 
1. DHS or any component thereof; 
2. Any employee of DHS in his/her 
official capacity; 
3. Any employee of DHS in his/her 
individual capacity where DOJ or DHS 
has agreed to represent the employee; or 
4. The U.S. or any agency thereof, is 
a party to the litigation or has an interest 
in such litigation, and DHS determines 
that the records are both relevant and 
necessary to the litigation and the use of 
such records is compatible with the 
purpose for which DHS collected the 
records. 
B. To a congressional office from the 
record of an individual in response to 
an inquiry from that congressional office 
made at the request of the individual to 
whom the record pertains. 
C. To the National Archives and 
Records Administration (NARA) or 
other Federal government agencies 
pursuant to records management 
inspections being conducted under the 
authority of 44 U.S.C. 2904 and 2906. 
D. To an agency, organization, or 
individual for the purpose of performing 
audit or oversight operations as 
authorized by law, but only such 
information as is necessary and relevant 
to such audit or oversight function. 
E. To appropriate agencies, entities, 
and persons when: 
1. DHS suspects or has confirmed that 
the security or confidentiality of 
information in the system of records has 
been compromised; 
2. DHS has determined that as a result 
of the suspected or confirmed 
compromise there is a risk of harm to 
economic or property interests, identity 
theft or fraud, or harm to the security or 
integrity of this system or other systems 
or programs (whether maintained by 
DHS or another agency or entity) or 
harm to the individual that rely upon 
the compromised information; and 
3. The disclosure made to such 
agencies, entities, and persons is 
reasonably necessary to assist in 
connection with DHS’s efforts to 
respond to the suspected or confirmed 
compromise and prevent, minimize, or 
remedy such harm. 
F. To contractors and their agents, 
grantees, experts, consultants, and 
others performing or working on a 
contract, service, grant, cooperative 
agreement, or other assignment for DHS, 
when necessary to accomplish an 
agency function related to this system of 
records. Individuals provided 
information under this routine use are 
subject to the same Privacy Act 
requirements and limitations on 
disclosure as are applicable to DHS 
officers and employees. 
G. To an appropriate Federal, state, 
Tribal, local, international, or foreign 
law enforcement agency or other 
appropriate authority charged with 
investigating or prosecuting a violation 
or enforcing or implementing a law,

record, either on its face or in 
conjunction with other information,

violation of law, which includes

consistent with the official duties of the

H. To approved Federal, state, and 
local government agencies for any 
legally mandated purpose in accordance 
with their authorizing statute or law and 
where an approved Memorandum of 
Agreement (MOA) or Computer

Abstract: The EPA promulgated the 
Air Emissions Reporting Requirements 
(AERR) (40 CFR part 51, subpart A) to 
coordinate emissions inventory 
reporting requirements. Under this 
reporting, 54 State and territorial air 
quality agencies, including the District 
of Columbia, as well as an estimated 9 
local air quality agencies, must submit 
emissions data every 3 years for all 
point sources and some non-point, onroad mobile, and non-road mobile 
sources of volatile organic compounds, 
oxides of nitrogen, carbon monoxide, 
sulfur dioxide, particulate matter less 
than or equal to 10 micrometers in 
diameter, particulate matter less than or 
equal to 2.5 micrometers in diameter, 
ammonia, and lead. In addition, the air 
quality agencies must submit annual 
emission data for point sources for a 
subset of point sources every year. An 
estimated 5 Tribal air agencies 
voluntarily submit point and nonpoint 
sources in triennial years. 
The data collected from the emission 
reporting is necessary to compile and 
make publicly available a national 
inventory of air pollutant emissions. 
The information collected supports both 
EPA’s implementation of the CAA, and 
State/Local/Tribal air agencies in 
fulfilling their requirements under CAA 
sections 110(a), 172, 182, 187, and 189 
to implement primary and secondary 
national ambient air quality standards 
(NAAQS). A comprehensive inventory 
updated at regular intervals is essential 
to allow the EPA to fulfill its mandate 
to monitor and plan for the attainment 
and maintenance of the NAAQS 
established for criteria pollutants in the 
CAA. 
Form Numbers: None. 
Respondents/affected entities: Entities 
potentially affected by this collection 
request are generally State, territorial, 
and local government air quality 
managements programs. Tribal 
governments are not affected unless 
they have sought and obtained 
‘‘Treatment as a State’’ (TAS) status 
under the Tribal Authority Rule and, on 
that basis, are authorized to implement 
and enforce the AERR rule. For the most 
recent 2023 triennial inventory, no 
Tribes have TAS for emissions 
inventory reporting, and 2 Tribal 
agencies voluntarily reported to the NEI. 
Additionally, State and local agencies 
collect data from owners/operators to be 
able to provide it to the EPA. The EPA 
seeks information from State and local 
air agencies to indicate the degree to 
which emissions data collection is due 
to the AERR rather than something that 
these agencies would impose even in 
the absence of the AERR. 
Respondent’s obligation to respond: 
This information is collected under 23 
U.S.C. 101; 42 U.S.C. 7401–7671q, and 
the authority of the AERR. This 
information is mandatory and, as 
specified, cannot be treated as 
confidential by the EPA. 
Estimated number of respondents: 68 
(total including voluntarily reporting) 
State, local and Tribal agencies and 
12,379 owners/operators reporting to 
State and local agencies. 
Frequency of response: Annual. 
Total estimated burden: 53,482 hours 
(per year) including 7,865 voluntary 
hours (per year) for State, local, and 
Tribal air agencies and 145,077 hours 
(per year) for owners/operators 
including 84 voluntary hours (per year). 
Burden is defined at 5 CFR 1320.03(b). 
Total estimated cost: $19,854,038 (per 
year) for State, local, and Tribal air 
agencies, which includes $712,432 for 
voluntary activities and $15,130,399 
annualized capital or operation and 
maintenance costs. $16,578,243 (per 
year) for owners/operators. 
Changes in the estimates: There is an 
increase of 4,780 hours in the total 
estimated respondent burden for State, 
local, and Tribal air agencies and an 
increase of 145,077 hours for owners/ 
operators compared with the ICR 
currently approved by OMB. This 
increase for State, local, and Tribal air 
agencies is due to improvements in the 
way the EPA estimates the burden. The 
increase for owners/operators is due to 
including the burden on owners/ 
operators for the first time in the 
approach.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
I. Background 
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 
1974, 5 U.S.C. 552a, the Department of 
Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. 
Citizenship and Immigration Services 
(USCIS) is proposing to modify and 
reissue a current DHS SORN titled, 
‘‘DHS/USCIS–004 Systematic Alien 
Verification for Entitlements Program 
System of Records.’’ 
This modified SORN is being 
published to update the purpose of 
SAVE to include the addition of 
expanded search functionality for 
registered SAVE user agencies to verify 
the U.S. citizenship of U.S. citizens by 
birth and to clarify use of SAVE for 
voter verification. 
This SORN modification also clarifies 
and informs the public that SAVE has 
removed transaction charges for all 
state, local, tribal, and territorial 
government agencies that use the 
system. Federal agencies are still 
charged a fee to use SAVE. 
DHS/USCIS is adding individuals that 
are U.S. citizens by birth to the 
categories of individuals covered by the 
system. 
DHS/USCIS is updating the categories 
of records in the system to include 
collecting both full and truncated (last 
four digits) Social Security number 
(other than those collected on Form G– 
845, Verification Request), U.S. passport 
number, driver’s license number, and 
information from the Social Security 
Administration. 
DHS/USCIS is revising the record 
source categories to add SSA–60–0058 
Master Files of Social Security Number 
Holders, Social Security Number 
Applications, February 20, 2025 (90 FR 
10025) and state or other national 
agencies that issue or maintain driver’s 
license information. 
DHS/USCIS is amending the routine 
uses section of the SORN to include 
adding Routine Use L, to support 
sharing with Social Security 
Administration and other federal 
organizations, and Routine Use M, to 
support sharing with federal agencies 
(e.g., the Department of Health and 
Human Services) to support auditing of 
federal programs administered by state, 
local, and tribal governments (e.g., 
Medicaid). 
Additionally, this notice includes 
non-substantive changes, including 
reorganizing of categories of records, 
change in the use of terms such as from 
‘‘derived’’ citizen/citizenship to 
‘‘acquired’’ citizen/citizenship, and 
spelling out of form names from the 
previously published system of records 
notice. 
Consistent with DHS’s information 
sharing mission, information stored in 
DHS/USCIS SAVE may be shared with 
other DHS Components that have a need 
to know of the information to carry out 
their national security, law enforcement, 
immigration, intelligence, or other 
homeland security functions. In 
addition, DHS/USCIS may share 
information with appropriate federal, 
state, local, tribal, territorial, foreign, or 
international government agencies 
consistent with the routine uses set 
forth in this system of records notice. 
Information in SAVE, including records 
submitted by the user agency, is not to 
be used for administrative (noncriminal) immigration enforcement 
purposes. See Immigration Reform and 
Control Act (IRCA), Public Law 99–603, 
Part C, Section 121(c)(1) (Nov. 6, 1986). 
This modified system will be 
included in DHS’s inventory of record 
systems. USCIS administers SAVE. 
SAVE is an online intergovernmental 
service designed to help federal, state, 
territorial, tribal, local government 
agencies, benefit-granting agencies, 
other authorized entities (e.g., Airport 
Operators under the Federal Aviation 
Administration (FAA) Extension, Safety 
and Security Act of 2016), and licensing 
bureaus, as authorized by law 
(collectively, ‘‘SAVE user agencies’’), 
determine the U.S. citizenship and 
immigration status of individuals within 
their jurisdiction for the purpose of 
granting benefits, licenses, and other 
lawful purposes. Uses of SAVE may 
include verification of immigration 
status or category and U.S citizenship, 
including U.S. citizens by birth as well 
as naturalized and certain acquired 
citizens, when issuing benefits such as 
Social Security numbers, public health 
care, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance 
Program payments, Temporary 
Assistance for Needy Families, 
Medicaid, Children’s Health Insurance 
Program; conducting background 
investigations, armed forces 
recruitment, REAL ID compliance; or 
any other purpose authorized by law, 
including verification of registrants and 
registered voters in voter registration 
and voter list maintenance processes. 
Prior to accessing SAVE, an agency 
must register as a user and enter into a 
Memorandum of Agreement with DHS/ 
USCIS. The prospective user provides 
the legal authorities requiring or 
permitting verification of immigration 
status or U.S. citizenship as part of 
issuing a benefit. SAVE does not 
determine a benefit applicant’s 
eligibility for a specific benefit. Only the 
user agency makes that determination. 
A typical SAVE verification involves 
a registered federal, state, territorial, 
tribal, or local government benefit or 
license-granting agency verifying the 
immigration status or U.S. citizenship of 
a benefit applicant. SAVE is not a 
database for immigration status and 
citizenship information. Rather, SAVE 
accesses the USCIS Verification Data 
Integration Service which searches 
multiple government databases or 
systems to provide a SAVE response. 
The initial SAVE response is derived 
from information contained in 
government systems accessed by SAVE 
using information from U.S. 
government-issued documents, such as 
a Social Security card, Permanent 
Resident Card (often referred to as a 
Green Card) or an Employment 
Authorization Document. For a SAVE 
user agency to create a SAVE case, the 
agency must collect and enter certain 
identifiers from the benefit applicant’s 
identity document(s). The verification 
process is driven by identifiers generally
